claim: Osteocalcin (OCN) is an osteoblast-derived hormone with pleiotropic physiological functions.
source: Osteocalcin (OCN) is an osteoblast-derived hormone with pleiotropic physiological functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about OCN supported by the broader scientific literature and context of the manuscript.

claim: OCN is subjected to post-translational modifications (PTMs) which control its activity.
source: Like many peptide hormones, OCN is subjected to post-translational modifications (PTMs) which control its activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by the manuscript's investigation and established knowledge about OCN.

claim: O-glycosylation is a novel PTM present on mouse OCN.
source: Here, we uncover O-glycosylation as a novel PTM present on mouse OCN and occurring on a single serine (S8) independently of its carboxylation and endoproteolysis, two other PTMs regulating this hormone.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by proteomics and cell-based assays described in the Results section.

claim: O-glycosylation of mouse OCN occurs on a single serine (S8).
source: Here, we uncover O-glycosylation as a novel PTM present on mouse OCN and occurring on a single serine (S8) independently of its carboxylation and endoproteolysis, two other PTMs regulating this hormone.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis studies and MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: O-glycosylation of mouse OCN occurs independently of its carboxylation.
source: Here, we uncover O-glycosylation as a novel PTM present on mouse OCN and occurring on a single serine (S8) independently of its carboxylation and endoproteolysis, two other PTMs regulating this hormone.
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figure 2C-E demonstrating that inhibition of carboxylation does not affect O-glycosylation.

claim: O-glycosylation of mouse OCN occurs independently of its endoproteolysis.
source: Here, we uncover O-glycosylation as a novel PTM present on mouse OCN and occurring on a single serine (S8) independently of its carboxylation and endoproteolysis, two other PTMs regulating this hormone.
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figure 2C-F demonstrating that inhibition of furin does not affect O-glycosylation.

claim: O-glycosylation increases OCN half-life in plasma ex vivo.
source: We also show that O-glycosylation increases OCN half-life in plasma ex vivo and in the circulation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability assays shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: O-glycosylation increases OCN half-life in the circulation in vivo.
source: We also show that O-glycosylation increases OCN half-life in plasma ex vivo and in the circulation in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo half-life experiments shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: In human OCN, the residue corresponding to S8 is a tyrosine (Y12).
source: Remarkably, in human OCN (hOCN), the residue corresponding to S8 is a tyrosine (Y12), which is not O-glycosylated.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Human OCN Y12 is not O-glycosylated.
source: Remarkably, in human OCN (hOCN), the residue corresponding to S8 is a tyrosine (Y12), which is not O-glycosylated.
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis and mass spectrometry shown in Figure 5B-F.

claim: The Y12S mutation is sufficient to O-glycosylate human OCN.
source: Yet, the Y12S mutation is sufficient to O-glycosylate hOCN and to increase its half-life in plasma compared to wildtype hOCN.
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5E.

claim: The Y12S mutation increases human OCN half-life in plasma compared to wildtype human OCN.
source: Yet, the Y12S mutation is sufficient to O-glycosylate hOCN and to increase its half-life in plasma compared to wildtype hOCN.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability assays shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Serum concentrations of OCN are higher in mouse than in human.
source: These findings reveal an important species difference in OCN regulation, which may explain why serum concentrations of OCN are higher in mouse than in human.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Table 1 comparing OCN levels across species and ages.

claim: OCN regulates glucose metabolism by promoting beta cell proliferation and insulin secretion.
source: It regulates glucose metabolism by promoting beta cell proliferation and insulin secretion, and by improving insulin sensitivity (Pi et al., 2011; Ferron et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: OCN regulates glucose metabolism by improving insulin sensitivity.
source: It regulates glucose metabolism by promoting beta cell proliferation and insulin secretion, and by improving insulin sensitivity (Pi et al., 2011; Ferron et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: OCN is involved in male fertility by promoting testosterone synthesis by Leydig cells.
source: In addition to its role in the regulation of energy metabolism, OCN is also involved in male fertility by promoting testosterone synthesis by Leydig cells (Oury et al., 2011), in muscle adaptation to exercise by improving glucose and fatty acid uptake in myocytes (Mera et al., 2016a), and in acute stress response through the inhibition of post-synaptic parasympathetic neurons (Berger et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Oury et al., 2011.

claim: OCN is involved in muscle adaptation to exercise by improving glucose and fatty acid uptake in myocytes.
source: In addition to its role in the regulation of energy metabolism, OCN is also involved in male fertility by promoting testosterone synthesis by Leydig cells (Oury et al., 2011), in muscle adaptation to exercise by improving glucose and fatty acid uptake in myocytes (Mera et al., 2016a), and in acute stress response through the inhibition of post-synaptic parasympathetic neurons (Berger et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mera et al., 2016a.

claim: OCN is involved in acute stress response through the inhibition of post-synaptic parasympathetic neurons.
source: In addition to its role in the regulation of energy metabolism, OCN is also involved in male fertility by promoting testosterone synthesis by Leydig cells (Oury et al., 2011), in muscle adaptation to exercise by improving glucose and fatty acid uptake in myocytes (Mera et al., 2016a), and in acute stress response through the inhibition of post-synaptic parasympathetic neurons (Berger et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Berger et al., 2019.

claim: OCN might act as an 'anti-geronic' circulating factor preventing age-related cognitive decline and muscle wasting.
source: Overall, OCN might acts as an 'anti-geronic' circulating factor preventing age-related cognitive decline and muscle wasting (Khrimian et al., 2017; Mera et al., 2016b; Oury et al., 2013b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies and uses speculative language ('might').

claim: GPRC6A mediates OCN function in beta cells, muscles and testis.
source: The G protein coupled receptor family C group six member A (GPRC6A) mediates OCN function in beta cells, muscles and testis (Mera et al., 2016a; Pi et al., 2011; Oury et al., 2013a), while the G protein coupled receptor 158 (Gpr158) mediates its function in the brain (Khrimian et al., 2017; Kosmidis et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gpr158 mediates OCN function in the brain.
source: The G protein coupled receptor family C group six member A (GPRC6A) mediates OCN function in beta cells, muscles and testis (Mera et al., 2016a; Pi et al., 2011; Oury et al., 2013a), while the G protein coupled receptor 158 (Gpr158) mediates its function in the brain (Khrimian et al., 2017; Kosmidis et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Prior to its secretion, in the osteoblast endoplasmic reticulum, the OCN precursor (pro-OCN) is γ-carboxylated on three glutamic acid residues by the vitamin K-dependent γ-glutamyl carboxylase.
source: Prior to its secretion, in the osteoblast endoplasmic reticulum, the OCN precursor (pro-OCN) is γ-carboxylated on three glutamic acid residues (Glu) by the vitamin K-dependent γ-glutamyl carboxylase (Ferron et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ferron et al., 2015.

claim: In the trans-Golgi network, pro-OCN is cleaved by the proprotein convertase furin releasing mature carboxylated OCN (Gla-OCN).
source: In the trans-Golgi network, pro-OCN is next cleaved by the proprotein convertase furin releasing mature carboxylated OCN (Gla-OCN) (Al Rifai et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Al Rifai et al., 2017.

claim: The presence of the negatively charged Gla residues allows Gla-OCN to bind hydroxyapatite, the mineral component of the bone extracellular matrix.
source: The presence of the negatively charged Gla residues allows Gla-OCN to bind hydroxyapatite, the mineral component of the bone extracellular matrix (ECM).
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the biochemical properties of Gla residues.

claim: During bone resorption, Gla-OCN is decarboxylated through a non-enzymatic process involving the acidic pH generated by the osteoclasts, ultimately leading to the release of bioactive uncarboxylated OCN (ucOCN) in the circulation.
source: It is during bone resorption that Gla-OCN is decarboxylated through a non-enzymatic process involving the acidic pH generated by the osteoclasts, ultimately leading to the release of bioactive uncarboxylated OCN (ucOCN) in the circulation (Ferron et al., 2010a; Lacombe et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ucOCN represents the bioactive form of OCN in rodents.
source: The conclusion that ucOCN represents the bioactive form of this protein in rodents is supported by cell-based assays, mouse genetics and in vivo studies [reviewed in Mera et al., 2018].
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The role of OCN in the regulation of glucose metabolism appears to be conserved in humans.
source: The role of OCN in the regulation of glucose metabolism appears to be conserved in humans.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent evidence presented in the paragraph.

claim: Human ucOCN can bind and activate human GPRC6A.
source: Human ucOCN can bind and activate human GPRC6A (De Toni et al., 2016) and promotes beta cell proliferation and insulin synthesis in human islets (Sabek et al., 2015), while mutations or polymorphisms in human GPRC6A are associated with insulin resistance (Di Nisio et al., 2017; Oury et al., 2013a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to De Toni et al., 2016.

claim: Human ucOCN promotes beta cell proliferation and insulin synthesis in human islets.
source: Human ucOCN can bind and activate human GPRC6A (De Toni et al., 2016) and promotes beta cell proliferation and insulin synthesis in human islets (Sabek et al., 2015), while mutations or polymorphisms in human GPRC6A are associated with insulin resistance (Di Nisio et al., 2017; Oury et al., 2013a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sabek et al., 2015.

claim: Mutations or polymorphisms in human GPRC6A are associated with insulin resistance.
source: Human ucOCN can bind and activate human GPRC6A (De Toni et al., 2016) and promotes beta cell proliferation and insulin synthesis in human islets (Sabek et al., 2015), while mutations or polymorphisms in human GPRC6A are associated with insulin resistance (Di Nisio et al., 2017; Oury et al., 2013a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Di Nisio et al., 2017 and Oury et al., 2013a.

claim: Several cross-sectional and observational studies have detected a negative association between OCN or ucOCN, and insulin resistance or the risk of developing type 2 diabetes in various human populations.
source: Finally, several cross-sectional and observational studies have detected a negative association between OCN or ucOCN, and insulin resistance or the risk of developing type 2 diabetes in various human populations (Lin et al., 2018; Turcotte et al., 2020; Lacombe et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Only 30 out of the 46 amino acids (i.e. 65%) composing mature mouse OCN are conserved in human OCN.
source: First, only 30 out of the 46 amino acids (i.e. 65%) composing mature mouse OCN are conserved in human OCN.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Leptin sequence displays about 85% conservation between mouse and human.
source: This is in striking contrast with other peptide hormones involved in the control of energy metabolism such as leptin and insulin whose respective sequence display about 85% conservation between mouse and human.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sequence conservation.

claim: Insulin sequence displays about 85% conservation between mouse and human.
source: This is in striking contrast with other peptide hormones involved in the control of energy metabolism such as leptin and insulin whose respective sequence display about 85% conservation between mouse and human.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sequence conservation.

claim: The circulating concentrations of OCN decrease with age in both mice and humans.
source: Second, the circulating concentrations of OCN, even though decreasing with age in both species, are five to ten times higher in mice than in humans throughout life span [(Mera et al., 2016a) see also Table 1].
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 and citation to Mera et al., 2016a.

claim: The circulating concentrations of OCN are five to ten times higher in mice than in humans throughout life span.
source: Second, the circulating concentrations of OCN, even though decreasing with age in both species, are five to ten times higher in mice than in humans throughout life span [(Mera et al., 2016a) see also Table 1].
evidence: This is supported by data in Table 1 and citation to Mera et al., 2016a.

claim: Serum OCN level is five- to ten-time lower in humans than in mice throughout life.
source: This analysis reveals that serum OCN level is five- to ten-time lower in humans than in mice throughout life.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: The most abundant OCN forms have a monoisotopic mass ranging from 5767.6961 to 6441.7636 Da.
source: This 'top-down' analysis revealed that the most abundant OCN forms have a monoisotopic mass ranging from 5767.6961 to 6441.7636 Da which exceeds the predicted mass of 5243.45 Da corresponding to the fully carboxylated (3 × Gla) OCN (Table 2 and Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: The monoisotopic mass of most abundant OCN forms exceeds the predicted mass of 5243.45 Da corresponding to the fully carboxylated (3 × Gla) OCN.
source: This 'top-down' analysis revealed that the most abundant OCN forms have a monoisotopic mass ranging from 5767.6961 to 6441.7636 Da which exceeds the predicted mass of 5243.45 Da corresponding to the fully carboxylated (3 × Gla) OCN (Table 2 and Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: The difference in monoisotopic mass could be mainly explained by the presence of a single O-linked glycan adduct composed of one N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc), one galactose (Gal) and one or two N-acetylneuraminic acid (NANA).
source: According to the various monoisotopic masses observed, we predict that this difference could be mainly explained by the presence of a single O-linked glycan adduct composed of one N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc), one galactose (Gal) and one or two N-acetylneuraminic acid (NANA).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mass spectrometry data presented in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: Uncarboxylated OCN does not accumulate in bone ECM.
source: Uncarboxylated OCN does not accumulate in bone ECM (Ferron et al., 2015) and accordingly, only fully or partially carboxylated OCN was detected in bone extracts, both of which were found to be O-glycosylated.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ferron et al., 2015 and data in Table 3.

claim: Only fully or partially carboxylated OCN was detected in bone extracts.
source: Uncarboxylated OCN does not accumulate in bone ECM (Ferron et al., 2015) and accordingly, only fully or partially carboxylated OCN was detected in bone extracts, both of which were found to be O-glycosylated.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Table 3.

claim: Both fully and partially carboxylated OCN detected in bone extracts were found to be O-glycosylated.
source: Uncarboxylated OCN does not accumulate in bone ECM (Ferron et al., 2015) and accordingly, only fully or partially carboxylated OCN was detected in bone extracts, both of which were found to be O-glycosylated.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Table 3.

claim: Significant amount of ucOCN could be detected in osteoblast culture supernatants.
source: In contrast, significant amount of ucOCN could be detected in osteoblast culture supernatants, most likely due to the low level of vitamin K present in fetal bovine serum.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Table 2.

claim: The O-linked glycan adduct could be detected on both carboxylated and uncarboxylated OCN in osteoblast supernatant.
source: Importantly, in osteoblast supernatant the O-linked glycan adduct could be detected on both carboxylated and uncarboxylated OCN (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Table 2.

claim: Mature mouse OCN contains three serine (S) and three threonine (T) residues.
source: Mature mouse OCN contains three serine (S) and three threonine (T) residues (Figure 1E), the two main types of amino acids on which O-glycosylation occurs (Steentoft et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on the amino acid sequence shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Serine and threonine are the two main types of amino acids on which O-glycosylation occurs.
source: Mature mouse OCN contains three serine (S) and three threonine (T) residues (Figure 1E), the two main types of amino acids on which O-glycosylation occurs (Steentoft et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Steentoft et al., 2013.

claim: Mutating all serine and threonine residues into alanine abrogates OCN glycosylation in primary mouse osteoblasts.
source: As expected, mutating all serine and threonine residues into alanine abrogates OCN glycosylation in primary mouse osteoblasts as assessed by SDS-PAGE (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The O-glycosylation site resides within the N-terminal part of the protein, that is on S5, S8 or T15.
source: Further mutagenesis studies revealed that the O-glycosylation site resides within the N-terminal part of the protein, that is on S5, S8 or T15 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Single amino acid mutagenesis allowed the identification of S8 as the O-glycosylation site of OCN in osteoblasts.
source: Single amino acid mutagenesis allowed the identification of S8 as the O-glycosylation site of OCN in osteoblasts (Figure 1G), a result consistent with the MS/MS analysis of OCN isolated from bone which also suggested that this residue is the O-glycosylation site (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data in Figure 1G and MS/MS data in Figure 1H.

claim: MS/MS analysis of OCN isolated from bone suggested that S8 is the O-glycosylation site.
source: Single amino acid mutagenesis allowed the identification of S8 as the O-glycosylation site of OCN in osteoblasts (Figure 1G), a result consistent with the MS/MS analysis of OCN isolated from bone which also suggested that this residue is the O-glycosylation site (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by MS/MS data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Mouse OCN is O-glycosylated on at least one serine residue in cell culture and in vivo.
source: Together, these results establish that mouse OCN is O-glycosylated on at least one serine residue in cell culture and in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 1 and Tables 2-3.

claim: Protein O-glycosylation is initiated by the transfer of a GalNAc to a serine or threonine residue.
source: Protein O-glycosylation is initiated by the transfer of a GalNAc to a serine or threonine residue, a reaction taking place in the Golgi and catalyzed by GalNAc-Ts, a family of enzymes comprising 19 different members in mice (Bennett et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bennett et al., 2012 and represents established knowledge.

claim: GalNAc-Ts are a family of enzymes comprising 19 different members in mice.
source: Protein O-glycosylation is initiated by the transfer of a GalNAc to a serine or threonine residue, a reaction taking place in the Golgi and catalyzed by GalNAc-Ts, a family of enzymes comprising 19 different members in mice (Bennett et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bennett et al., 2012.

claim: Several GalNAc-Ts are expressed in primary mouse osteoblasts.
source: Quantitative PCR on mRNA isolated from undifferentiated and differentiated primary mouse osteoblasts revealed that several GalNAc-Ts are expressed in this cell type, with Galnt1 and Galnt2 being the most strongly expressed ones (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Galnt1 and Galnt2 are the most strongly expressed GalNAc-Ts in primary mouse osteoblasts.
source: Quantitative PCR on mRNA isolated from undifferentiated and differentiated primary mouse osteoblasts revealed that several GalNAc-Ts are expressed in this cell type, with Galnt1 and Galnt2 being the most strongly expressed ones (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: S8A mutation abrogates OCN O-glycosylation in HEK293 cells.
source: We noticed that S8A mutation abrogates OCN O-glycosylation in HEK293 cells and in primary osteoblasts (Figure 1G and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: S8A mutation abrogates OCN O-glycosylation in primary osteoblasts.
source: We noticed that S8A mutation abrogates OCN O-glycosylation in HEK293 cells and in primary osteoblasts (Figure 1G and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: GalNAc-T3 and GalNAc-T6 are expressed in HEK293.
source: GalNAc-T3 and its paralogue GalNAc-T6 are known to be expressed in HEK293 (Narimatsu et al., 2019b) and our data shows they are also expressed in primary mouse osteoblasts and induced during osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Narimatsu et al., 2019b.

claim: GalNAc-T3 and GalNAc-T6 are expressed in primary mouse osteoblasts and induced during osteoblast differentiation.
source: GalNAc-T3 and its paralogue GalNAc-T6 are known to be expressed in HEK293 (Narimatsu et al., 2019b) and our data shows they are also expressed in primary mouse osteoblasts and induced during osteoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The inactivation of GALNT3 and/or GALNT6 genes failed to alter OCN O-glycosylation in HEK293.
source: Although these observations suggest one or both of these enzymes may be involved in OCN O-glycosylation, the inactivation of GALNT3 and/or GALNT6 genes failed to alter OCN O-glycosylation in HEK293 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Inactivation of GALNT1, GALNT2, and GALNT3 genes partially abolished OCN glycosylation in HEK293 cells.
source: Since GALNT1 and GALNT2 are also highly expressed in osteoblasts and induced during osteoblast differentiation, we inactivated these two genes in combination with GALNT3, and assess the impact on OCN O-glycosylation in HEK293 cells. This partially abolished OCN glycosylation (Figure 2B), suggesting that these three GalNAc-Ts are the primary isoenzymes that redundantly initiate the O-glycosylation of OCN.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GALNT1, GALNT2, and GALNT3 are the primary isoenzymes that redundantly initiate the O-glycosylation of OCN.
source: Since GALNT1 and GALNT2 are also highly expressed in osteoblasts and induced during osteoblast differentiation, we inactivated these two genes in combination with GALNT3, and assess the impact on OCN O-glycosylation in HEK293 cells. This partially abolished OCN glycosylation (Figure 2B), suggesting that these three GalNAc-Ts are the primary isoenzymes that redundantly initiate the O-glycosylation of OCN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knockout data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of γ-carboxylation or furin did not impact OCN O-glycosylation in primary osteoblasts and HEK293 cells.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of γ-carboxylation or furin, using warfarin or Dec-RVKR-CMK (RVKR) respectively, did not impact OCN O-glycosylation in primary osteoblasts and HEK293 cells (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of OCN O-glycosylation through GalNAc-bn treatment or the S8A mutation did not significantly affect its processing or its γ-carboxylation.
source: Similarly, inhibition of OCN O-glycosylation through GalNAc-bn treatment or the S8A mutation did not significantly affect its processing or its γ-carboxylation (Figure 2C–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and ELISA data shown in Figure 2C-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both mature OCN present in control bones and pro-OCN present in furin-deficient bones are de-glycosylated by neuraminidase and O-glycosidase.
source: As shown in Figure 2F, both mature OCN present in control bones and pro-OCN present in furin-deficient bones are de-glycosylated by neuraminidase and O-glycosidase, indicating that pro-OCN is normally O-glycosylated in absence of processing by furin in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Pro-OCN is normally O-glycosylated in absence of processing by furin in vivo.
source: As shown in Figure 2F, both mature OCN present in control bones and pro-OCN present in furin-deficient bones are de-glycosylated by neuraminidase and O-glycosidase, indicating that pro-OCN is normally O-glycosylated in absence of processing by furin in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Osteocalcin O-glycosylation is not affected by its carboxylation status or by its processing by furin.
source: Altogether, these results support the notion that osteocalcin O-glycosylation is not affected by its carboxylation status or by its processing by furin.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Blocking O-glycosylation does not prevent pro-OCN processing by furin or its carboxylation.
source: Moreover, blocking O-glycosylation does not prevent pro-OCN processing by furin or its carboxylation.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 2C-E.

claim: O-glycosylation can increase the stability of some peptide hormones in the circulation by preventing proteolytic degradation.
source: It was recently observed that O-glycosylation can also increase the stability of some peptide hormones in the circulation by preventing proteolytic degradation (Hansen et al., 2019; Madsen et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hansen et al., 2019 and Madsen et al., 2020.

claim: >99% of the ucOCN purified from HEK293 is O-glycosylated.
source: Importantly, we observed that >99% of the ucOCN purified from HEK293 is O-glycosylated, with a certain proportion (~30%) containing two glycan adducts (Figure 3A), suggesting that in this context O-glycosylation may occurs on more than one residue.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A certain proportion (~30%) of ucOCN purified from HEK293 contains two glycan adducts.
source: Importantly, we observed that >99% of the ucOCN purified from HEK293 is O-glycosylated, with a certain proportion (~30%) containing two glycan adducts (Figure 3A), suggesting that in this context O-glycosylation may occurs on more than one residue.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the context of HEK293 expression, O-glycosylation may occur on more than one residue.
source: Importantly, we observed that >99% of the ucOCN purified from HEK293 is O-glycosylated, with a certain proportion (~30%) containing two glycan adducts (Figure 3A), suggesting that in this context O-glycosylation may occurs on more than one residue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mass spectrometry data showing two glycan adducts.

claim: Non-glycosylated ucOCN has a half-life of ~120 min when incubated in plasma at 37°C.
source: Non-glycosylated ucOCN has a half-life of ~120 min when incubated in plasma at 37°C, while O-glycosylated ucOCN is stable for more than 5 hr in the same conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: O-glycosylated ucOCN is stable for more than 5 hr when incubated in plasma at 37°C.
source: Non-glycosylated ucOCN has a half-life of ~120 min when incubated in plasma at 37°C, while O-glycosylated ucOCN is stable for more than 5 hr in the same conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Non-glycosylated ucOCN was stable when incubated in a saline solution containing 3.5% BSA at 37°C for 2 hr.
source: Non-glycosylated ucOCN was stable when incubated in a saline solution containing 3.5% BSA at 37°C for 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), implying that ucOCN is not intrinsically unstable.
evidence: This is supported by stability data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: ucOCN is not intrinsically unstable.
source: Non-glycosylated ucOCN was stable when incubated in a saline solution containing 3.5% BSA at 37°C for 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), implying that ucOCN is not intrinsically unstable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Stability of the non-glycosylated ucOCN was restored when incubated in plasma at 4°C or in heat-inactivated (HI) plasma at 37°C.
source: In addition, stability of the non-glycosylated ucOCN was restored when incubated in plasma at 4°C or in heat-inactivated (HI) plasma at 37°C (Figure 3D), suggesting that non-glycosylated ucOCN's decline involves the action of a protease.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Non-glycosylated ucOCN's decline involves the action of a protease.
source: In addition, stability of the non-glycosylated ucOCN was restored when incubated in plasma at 4°C or in heat-inactivated (HI) plasma at 37°C (Figure 3D), suggesting that non-glycosylated ucOCN's decline involves the action of a protease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Pepstatin A, RVKR, and EDTA did not affect non-glycosylated ucOCN stability in plasma ex vivo.
source: Pepstatin A (Pep A) an aspartic proteases inhibitor, RVKR a proprotein convertases inhibitor and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) which inhibits metalloproteases did not affect non-glycosylated ucOCN stability in plasma ex vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The OCN sequence surrounding S8 contains several proline residues.
source: The OCN sequence surrounding S8 contains several proline residues (Figure 1E) and could therefore be recognized by prolyl endopeptidases, such as the fibroblast activation protein (FAP) which is present in the circulation (Sánchez-Garrido et al., 2016; Coutts et al., 1996).
evidence: This is based on the amino acid sequence shown in Figure 1E.

claim: FAP is present in the circulation.
source: The OCN sequence surrounding S8 contains several proline residues (Figure 1E) and could therefore be recognized by prolyl endopeptidases, such as the fibroblast activation protein (FAP) which is present in the circulation (Sánchez-Garrido et al., 2016; Coutts et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sánchez-Garrido et al., 2016 and Coutts et al., 1996.

claim: Treatment of plasma with 10 mM talabostat increased non-glycosylated ucOCN degradation.
source: Surprisingly, treatment of plasma with 10 mM talabostat did not inhibit, but rather increased non-glycosylated ucOCN degradation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A reduced stability of non-glycosylated OCN in plasma was observed in the presence of PMSF.
source: A reduced stability of non-glycosylated OCN in plasma was also observed in the presence of PMSF (Figure 3F) at a concentration (10 mM) that was also shown to inhibit dipeptidyl peptidases and prolyl endopeptidases (Banbula et al., 2000; Bermpohl et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: One function of FAP in vivo is to activate the α2-antiplasmin precursor releasing the active α2-antiplasmin, which in turn acts as an inhibitor of plasmin activity.
source: One function of FAP in vivo is to activate the α2-antiplasmin precursor releasing the active α2-antiplasmin, which in turn acts as an inhibitor of plasmin activity (Lee et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2011 and Lee et al., 2006.

claim: Mouse OCN contains arginine residues in its N- and C-terminus (R16 and R40, respectively), which could be potential cleavage sites for plasmin.
source: Interestingly, mouse OCN contains arginine residues in its N- and C-terminus (R16 and R40, respectively), which could be potential cleavage sites for plasmin (Rawlings et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on the amino acid sequence and citation to Rawlings et al., 2008.

claim: ucOCN is rapidly degraded when low concentration of recombinant plasmin is added to previously heat-inactivated plasma or in Tris buffered solution.
source: Supporting this notion, ucOCN is rapidly degraded when low concentration of recombinant plasmin is added to previously heat-inactivated plasma or in Tris buffered solution (Figure 3G and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by plasmin enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: O-glycosylation partially protects ucOCN from plasmin-mediated degradation.
source: Moreover, O-glycosylation partially protect ucOCN from plasmin-mediated degradation in the same assay (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by plasmin enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: O-glycosylation protects ucOCN from plasmin mediated proteolysis, thereby increasing its half-life in plasma in vitro.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that O-glycosylation protects ucOCN from plasmin mediated proteolysis, thereby increasing its half-life in plasma in vitro.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Following an injection of 40 ng/g of body weight of ucOCN in fasted animals, the level of glycosylated ucOCN remains higher compared to the non-glycosylated form for the following 90 min.
source: In fasted animals, following an injection of 40 ng/g of body weight of ucOCN, the level of glycosylated ucOCN remains higher compared to the non-glycosylated form for the following 90 min (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo half-life data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The concentration of non-glycosylated OCN declines more rapidly than the one of glycosylated ucOCN when expressed as a percentage of the maximum concentration reached at 30 min.
source: Moreover, when expressed as a percentage of the maximum concentration reached at 30 min, the concentration of non-glycosylated OCN declines more rapidly than the one of glycosylated ucOCN (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo half-life data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The in vivo half-life of O-glycosylated ucOCN is estimated to be ~182 min.
source: Based on these curves, we estimated the in vivo half-life of O-glycosylated and non-glycosylated ucOCN to ~182 and~108 min respectively.
evidence: This is an estimation based on the in vivo half-life data shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: The in vivo half-life of non-glycosylated ucOCN is estimated to be ~108 min.
source: Based on these curves, we estimated the in vivo half-life of O-glycosylated and non-glycosylated ucOCN to ~182 and~108 min respectively.
evidence: This is an estimation based on the in vivo half-life data shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: In fed mice, glycosylated ucOCN serum concentration remains higher than the one of non-glycosylated ucOCN for up to 2 hr following an injection of 40 ng/g of body weight.
source: In fed mice, glycosylated ucOCN serum concentration also remains higher than the one of non-glycosylated ucOCN for up to 2 hr following an injection of 40 ng/g of body weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo stability data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Circulating level of glycosylated ucOCN after 2 hr was further increased when 80 ng/g of body weight of protein was injected.
source: Circulating level of glycosylated ucOCN after 2 hr was further increased when 80 ng/g of body weight of protein was injected, while non-glycosylated ucOCN was not significantly increased with this higher dose (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo stability data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Non-glycosylated ucOCN was not significantly increased with a higher dose of 80 ng/g of body weight.
source: Circulating level of glycosylated ucOCN after 2 hr was further increased when 80 ng/g of body weight of protein was injected, while non-glycosylated ucOCN was not significantly increased with this higher dose (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo stability data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: O-glycosylation increases the stability of mouse OCN protein in vivo.
source: These results establish that O-glycosylation increases the stability of mouse OCN protein in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the in vivo data presented in Figure 3H-I and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: INS-1 832/3 cells express GPRC6A and respond to OCN.
source: INS-1 832/3 cells, a sub-clone of the INS-1 rat insulinoma cell line previously shown to express GPRC6A and to respond to OCN (Ferron et al., 2010a; Pi et al., 2016), were treated with vehicle or low doses of non-glycosylated and glycosylated ucOCN for 8 hr.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ferron et al., 2010a and Pi et al., 2016.

claim: Non-glycosylated ucOCN stimulation at 0.3 ng/ml could increase Ins1 expression by 1.5-fold.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, non-glycosylated ucOCN stimulation at 0.3 ng/ml could increase Ins1 expression by 1.5-fold.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A lower dose of glycosylated ucOCN (0.1 ng/ml) was sufficient to significantly increase the expression of Ins1 as compared to vehicle or to 0.3 ng/ml non-glycosylated ucOCN stimulation.
source: However, a lower dose of glycosylated ucOCN (0.1 ng/ml) was sufficient to significantly increase the expression of Ins1 as compared to vehicle or to 0.3 ng/ml non-glycosylated ucOCN stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The difference in biological activity between glycosylated and non-glycosylated ucOCN could be explained at least in part by an increased stability of glycosylated ucOCN as compared to non-glycosylated ucOCN in INS-1 832/3 cell cultures.
source: These difference in biological activity could be explained at least in part by an increased stability of glycosylated ucOCN as compared to non-glycosylated ucOCN in INS-1 832/3 cell cultures (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an inference supported by stability data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Glycosylated ucOCN is biologically active in the setting of a cell-based assay.
source: Overall, these results suggest that glycosylated ucOCN is biologically active, at least in the setting of this cell-based assay, and that O-glycosylation also increases the stability of ucOCN in cell culture.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: O-glycosylation increases the stability of ucOCN in cell culture.
source: Overall, these results suggest that glycosylated ucOCN is biologically active, at least in the setting of this cell-based assay, and that O-glycosylation also increases the stability of ucOCN in cell culture.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Mature human OCN does not contain the O-glycosylation site found in the mouse protein.
source: In contrast, mature human OCN does not contain the O-glycosylation site found in the mouse protein and consequently is not normally glycosylated.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5A and western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: Mature human OCN is not normally glycosylated.
source: In contrast, mature human OCN does not contain the O-glycosylation site found in the mouse protein and consequently is not normally glycosylated.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5B-F.

claim: Mouse and human ucOCN have a very similar predicted molecular weight, that is 5.1 and 5.8 kDa, respectively.
source: Since mouse and human ucOCN have a very similar predicted molecular weight, that is 5.1 and 5.8 kDa, respectively, these observations suggested that human OCN may not be O-glycosylated.
evidence: This is based on molecular weight calculations.

claim: Introduction of a single serine residue (Y12S mutation) in the human protein is sufficient to induce its O-glycosylation in osteoblasts.
source: Remarkably, introduction of a single serine residue (Y12S mutation) in the human protein is sufficient to induce its O-glycosylation in osteoblasts as visualized by western blot (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Introducing a leucine at position Y12 (Y12L) did not alter human OCN apparent molecular weight.
source: In contrast, introducing a leucine at the same position (Y12L) did not alter human OCN apparent molecular weight, indicating that this tyrosine residue is not normally subjected to O-glycosylation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The tyrosine residue at position Y12 is not normally subjected to O-glycosylation.
source: In contrast, introducing a leucine at the same position (Y12L) did not alter human OCN apparent molecular weight, indicating that this tyrosine residue is not normally subjected to O-glycosylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: O-glycosylation does not affect human OCN processing by furin.
source: Since the apparent molecular weight of both native and Y12S human OCN are increased following treatment with RVKR, we concluded that O-glycosylation does not affect human OCN processing by furin (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mature human OCN is not normally subjected to O-glycosylation.
source: These results establish that mature human OCN is not normally subjected to O-glycosylation, but that a single amino acid change (Y12S) is sufficient to induce its O-glycosylation in osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 5B-D.

claim: A single amino acid change (Y12S) is sufficient to induce human OCN O-glycosylation in osteoblasts.
source: These results establish that mature human OCN is not normally subjected to O-glycosylation, but that a single amino acid change (Y12S) is sufficient to induce its O-glycosylation in osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Human ucOCN containing the Y12S mutation purified from HEK293 was found to be O-glycosylated.
source: Confirming what was observed in osteoblasts, human ucOCN containing the Y12S mutation purified from HEK293 was found to be O-glycosylated (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Non-glycosylated human ucOCN level declines by 50% within 180 min when incubated in Bglap-/- mouse plasma at 37°C.
source: As shown in Figure 5G, in the conditions of this assay, non-glycosylated human ucOCN level declines by 50% within 180 min, while the concentration of the O-glycosylated version remains stable over the course of the experiment (i.e. 5 hr).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The concentration of O-glycosylated human ucOCN remains stable over 5 hr when incubated in Bglap-/- mouse plasma at 37°C.
source: As shown in Figure 5G, in the conditions of this assay, non-glycosylated human ucOCN level declines by 50% within 180 min, while the concentration of the O-glycosylated version remains stable over the course of the experiment (i.e. 5 hr).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Human ucOCN degradation was only inhibited when the plasma was heat-inactivated or incubated at 4°C.
source: As observed with the mouse protein, human ucOCN degradation was only inhibited when the plasma was heat-inactivated or incubated at 4°C (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that glycosylation protects mouse and human ucOCN from degradation through a similar mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo plasma stability data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Glycosylation protects mouse and human ucOCN from degradation through a similar mechanism.
source: As observed with the mouse protein, human ucOCN degradation was only inhibited when the plasma was heat-inactivated or incubated at 4°C (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting that glycosylation protects mouse and human ucOCN from degradation through a similar mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of the ex vivo plasma stability data for mouse and human ucOCN.

claim: O-glycosylation is a novel PTM regulating mouse ucOCN half-life in the circulation.
source: In this study we identified O-glycosylation as a novel PTM regulating mouse ucOCN half-life in the circulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: O-glycosylation is not found on human mature OCN.
source: We also showed that O-glycosylation is not found on human mature OCN, but that O-glycosylation of human OCN by means of a single amino acid change can improve its half-life in plasma ex vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: O-glycosylation of human OCN by means of a single amino acid change can improve its half-life in plasma ex vivo.
source: We also showed that O-glycosylation is not found on human mature OCN, but that O-glycosylation of human OCN by means of a single amino acid change can improve its half-life in plasma ex vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 5G-H.

claim: These findings reveal an important species difference in the regulation of OCN.
source: These findings reveal an important species difference in the regulation of OCN and may also have important implication for the future use of recombinant ucOCN as a therapeutic agent in humans.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the implications of the findings.

claim: These findings may have important implication for the future use of recombinant ucOCN as a therapeutic agent in humans.
source: These findings reveal an important species difference in the regulation of OCN and may also have important implication for the future use of recombinant ucOCN as a therapeutic agent in humans.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: The initiation of O-glycosylation is catalyzed by the GalNAc-Ts isoenzymes.
source: The initiation of O-glycosylation is catalyzed by the GalNAc-Ts isoenzymes, however, the specific protein sequence(s) targeted by each of the GalNAc-Ts remain poorly characterized, although weak acceptor motifs for these have been identified by in vitro analyses (Perrine et al., 2009; Gerken et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Perrine et al., 2009 and Gerken et al., 2006.

claim: The specific protein sequence(s) targeted by each of the GalNAc-Ts remain poorly characterized.
source: The initiation of O-glycosylation is catalyzed by the GalNAc-Ts isoenzymes, however, the specific protein sequence(s) targeted by each of the GalNAc-Ts remain poorly characterized, although weak acceptor motifs for these have been identified by in vitro analyses (Perrine et al., 2009; Gerken et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Perrine et al., 2009 and Gerken et al., 2006.

claim: Mouse OCN is O-glycosylated likely on serine 8, which is located within the amino acid sequence SVPSPDP11.
source: Here, we demonstrate that mouse OCN is O-glycosylated likely on serine 8, which is located within the amino acid sequence SVPSPDP11.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the mutagenesis and MS/MS data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The sequence SVPSPDP11 strongly matches the consensus site previously defined for GalNAc-T1 and GalNAc-T2.
source: Interestingly, this sequence strongly matches the consensus site previously defined for GalNAc-T1 and GalNAc-T2 (Gerken et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gerken et al., 2006.

claim: The presence of proline residues in position −one, +one and +three has been shown to be determinant in the recognition of peptide substrates by GalNAc-T1 and GalNAc-T2 in vitro.
source: In particular, the presence of proline residues in position −one, +one and +three has been shown to be determinant in the recognition of peptide substrates by GalNAc-T1 and GalNAc-T2 in vitro.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about GalNAc-T substrate recognition.

claim: OCN may be a substrate for additional GalNAc-Ts beyond GalNAc-T1, 2, and 3.
source: Combined knock out of GalNAc-T1, 2 and 3 only partially abolishes mouse OCN O-glycosylation in HEK293 cells, suggesting that OCN may be a substrate for additional GalNAc-Ts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knockout data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: O-glycosylation was shown to interfere with the action of proprotein convertases on several pro-hormones and receptors.
source: O-glycosylation was shown to interfere with the action of proprotein convertases on several pro-hormones and receptors (Goth et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2006; May et al., 2003; Schjoldager and Clausen, 2012; Schjoldager et al., 2010; Goth et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: O-glycosylation does not interfere with pro-OCN processing by furin in vitro and in vivo.
source: This appears not to be the case for OCN as its O-glycosylation does not interfere with its processing by furin in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 2C-F.

claim: In other proteins, such as leptin and erythropoietin, glycosylation adducts were shown to increase protein stability and half-life in circulation.
source: In other proteins, such as leptin and erythropoietin, glycosylation adducts were shown to increase protein stability and half-life in circulation (Elliott et al., 2003; Creus et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Elliott et al., 2003 and Creus et al., 2001.

claim: O-glycosylation was shown to protect atrial natriuretic peptide from proteolytic degradation by neprilysin or insulin-degrading enzyme in vitro.
source: More recently, O-glycosylation was shown to protect atrial natriuretic peptide from proteolytic degradation by neprilysin or insulin-degrading enzyme in vitro (Hansen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hansen et al., 2019.

claim: Sialic acid residues present in the glycosylation adducts increase protein charge, thereby improving serum half-life and decreasing liver and renal clearance.
source: Additional studies showed that sialic acid residues present in the glycosylation adducts increase protein charge, thereby improving serum half-life and decreasing liver and renal clearance (Morell et al., 1971; Runkel et al., 1998; Perlman et al., 2003; Ziltener et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Protection from proteolytic cleavage by plasmin in the plasma might be one mechanism by which O-glycosylation extends OCN half-life.
source: Although our data suggest that protection from proteolytic cleavage by plasmin in the plasma might be one mechanism by which O-glycosylation extend OCN half-life, we cannot exclude that in vivo, O-glycosylation may also decrease liver and renal clearance of OCN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ex vivo and in vivo data presented in Figure 3.

claim: In vivo, O-glycosylation may also decrease liver and renal clearance of OCN.
source: Although our data suggest that protection from proteolytic cleavage by plasmin in the plasma might be one mechanism by which O-glycosylation extend OCN half-life, we cannot exclude that in vivo, O-glycosylation may also decrease liver and renal clearance of OCN.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential additional mechanisms.

claim: Mouse OCN contains arginine (R) residues at position 16 and 40.
source: Mouse OCN contains arginine (R) residues at position 16 and 40, corresponding to R20 and R44 in human OCN, which could be potential cleavage sites for plasmin (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on the amino acid sequence shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A putative plasmin cleavage site is present in mouse OCN at AYK↓R40.
source: A putative plasmin cleavage site is present in mouse (i.e. AYK↓R40, where the arrow indicates the cleavage site) and human (i.e. AYR↓R44) OCN at the corresponding position (Backes et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Backes et al., 2000.

claim: A putative plasmin cleavage site is present in human OCN at AYR↓R44.
source: A putative plasmin cleavage site is present in mouse (i.e. AYK↓R40, where the arrow indicates the cleavage site) and human (i.e. AYR↓R44) OCN at the corresponding position (Backes et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Backes et al., 2000.

claim: Bovine OCN does not possess the O-glycosylation site found in the mouse protein.
source: Bovine OCN, like the human protein, does not possess the O-glycosylation site found in mouse, and was shown to be cleaved by plasmin in vitro between R43 and R44 (Novak et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Novak et al., 1997.

claim: Bovine OCN was shown to be cleaved by plasmin in vitro between R43 and R44.
source: Bovine OCN, like the human protein, does not possess the O-glycosylation site found in mouse, and was shown to be cleaved by plasmin in vitro between R43 and R44 (Novak et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Novak et al., 1997.

claim: Plasmin is sufficient to reduce the concentration of non-glycosylated ucOCN by more than 90% in two hours.
source: Here we show that plasmin is sufficient to reduce the concentration non-glycosylated ucOCN, by more than 90% in two hours, confirming that mouse ucOCN is also a plasmin substrate.
evidence: This is supported by plasmin enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Mouse ucOCN is a plasmin substrate.
source: Here we show that plasmin is sufficient to reduce the concentration non-glycosylated ucOCN, by more than 90% in two hours, confirming that mouse ucOCN is also a plasmin substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the plasmin enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: OCN serum levels are decreased in mice deficient in plasmin activator inhibitor I (PAI-I), which have higher plasmin activity.
source: Supporting a role for plasmin in the cleavage of mouse OCN in vivo, OCN serum levels are decreased in mice deficient in plasmin activator inhibitor I (PAI-I), which have higher plasmin activity (Tamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tamura et al., 2013.

claim: Circulating plasmin activity increases with age in rats and humans.
source: Interestingly, circulating plasmin activity increases with age in rats and humans (Paczek et al., 2009; Paczek et al., 2008), an observation which could in part explain the gradual reduction of serum OCN concentrations during aging (Mera et al., 2016a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Paczek et al., 2009 and Paczek et al., 2008.

claim: The gradual reduction of serum OCN concentrations during aging could in part be explained by increased circulating plasmin activity with age.
source: Interestingly, circulating plasmin activity increases with age in rats and humans (Paczek et al., 2009; Paczek et al., 2008), an observation which could in part explain the gradual reduction of serum OCN concentrations during aging (Mera et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting two observations.

claim: A nonsynonymous rare variant (rs34702397) in OCN resulting in the conversion of R43 to a glutamine (Q) exists in humans of African ancestry.
source: Notably, a nonsynonymous rare variant (rs34702397) in OCN resulting in the conversion of R43 in a glutamine (Q) exists in humans of African ancestry and was nominally associated with insulin sensitivity index and glucose disposal in a small cohort of African Americans (Das et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Das et al., 2010.

claim: The R43Q variant was nominally associated with insulin sensitivity index and glucose disposal in a small cohort of African Americans.
source: Notably, a nonsynonymous rare variant (rs34702397) in OCN resulting in the conversion of R43 in a glutamine (Q) exists in humans of African ancestry and was nominally associated with insulin sensitivity index and glucose disposal in a small cohort of African Americans (Das et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Das et al., 2010.

claim: The R43Q variant eliminates the potential plasmin cleavage site in the C-terminal region of human OCN.
source: Since the R43Q variant eliminates the potential plasmin cleavage site in the C-terminal region, it will be interesting to further investigate if subjects carrying this variant have higher OCN circulating levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence change and knowledge of plasmin cleavage sites.

claim: O-glycosylation protects mouse ucOCN from degradation in INS-1 cell cultures.
source: We also show that O-glycosylation protects mouse ucOCN from degradation in INS-1 cell cultures and consequently increases its biological activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: O-glycosylation increases mouse ucOCN biological activity in INS-1 cell cultures.
source: We also show that O-glycosylation protects mouse ucOCN from degradation in INS-1 cell cultures and consequently increases its biological activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Non-glycosylated ucOCN is stable when incubated in the INS-1 cell culture media at 37°C without cells.
source: Interestingly, non-glycosylated ucOCN is stable when incubated in the INS-1 cell culture media at 37°C without cells (data not shown), suggesting that the proteolytic activity originates from the INS-1 cells and not from the culture media.
evidence: This is based on unpublished data mentioned in the text.

claim: The proteolytic activity responsible for ucOCN degradation in INS-1 cell cultures originates from the INS-1 cells and not from the culture media.
source: Interestingly, non-glycosylated ucOCN is stable when incubated in the INS-1 cell culture media at 37°C without cells (data not shown), suggesting that the proteolytic activity originates from the INS-1 cells and not from the culture media.
evidence: This is an inference based on unpublished data mentioned in the text.

claim: Plasmin is expressed exclusively by the hepatocytes.
source: The identity of a putative β-cell-derived protease responsible for ucOCN degradation remains unknown, since plasmin is expressed exclusively by the hepatocytes.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about plasmin expression.

claim: Human OCN is not subjected to O-glycosylation.
source: We found that human OCN is not subjected to O-glycosylation and that consequently it has a reduced half-life in plasma ex vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 5B-F.

claim: Human OCN has a reduced half-life in plasma ex vivo compared to glycosylated mouse OCN.
source: We found that human OCN is not subjected to O-glycosylation and that consequently it has a reduced half-life in plasma ex vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: The O-glycosylation sequence 'SVPSPDP11' of mouse OCN is conserved in the human protein, except for the amino acids corresponding to S5 and S8, which are replaced by a proline (P9) and a tyrosine (Y12).
source: The O-glycosylation sequence 'SVPSPDP11' of mouse OCN is conserved in the human protein, except for the amino acids corresponding to S5 and S8, which are replaced by a proline (P9) and a tyrosine (Y12) (i.e. 'PVPYPDP15').
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5A.

claim: O-glycosylated human OCN is protected from degradation in plasma ex vivo similarly to the glycosylated mouse protein.
source: Remarkably, we could introduce O-glycosylation into human OCN by a single amino acid change (Y12S). O-glycosylated human OCN is protected from degradation in plasma ex vivo similarly to the glycosylated mouse protein.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 5G-H.

claim: The difference in the O-glycosylation status of OCN could potentially explain why circulating level of OCN in 1- to 6-month-old mice is 5–10 times higher than the level measured in young or adult human.
source: Hence, this difference in the O-glycosylation status of OCN could potentially explain why circulating level of OCN in 1- to 6-month-old mice is 5–10 times higher than the level measured in young or adult human (Table 1).
evidence: This is a speculative inference connecting the O-glycosylation difference to the observed difference in circulating levels.

claim: It remains unknown if the increased half-life of O-glycosylated ucOCN will result in improved biological activity in vivo.
source: It remains unknown if the increased half-life of O-glycosylated ucOCN will result in improved biological activity in vivo, although it was shown to be the case for other proteins (Baudys et al., 1995; Runkel et al., 1998; Elliott et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging uncertainty, with citations to studies on other proteins.

claim: More than 80% of OCN, including the ucOCN fraction, is O-glycosylated in osteoblast supernatant and in serum.
source: We also showed that mouse OCN is endogenously O-glycosylated in vivo and that more than 80% of OCN, including the ucOCN fraction, is O-glycosylated in osteoblast supernatant and in serum.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: The bioactive form of OCN is O-glycosylated in vivo in mice.
source: This suggests that the bioactive form of OCN is O-glycosylated in vivo in mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that most OCN is O-glycosylated in vivo.

claim: This work identified O-glycosylation as a previously unrecognized OCN PTM regulating its half-life in circulation in mice.
source: In summary, this work identified O-glycosylation as a previously unrecognized OCN PTM regulating its half-life in circulation in mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: Introducing O-glycosylation in human ucOCN increases its half-life in plasma.
source: This modification is not conserved in human, yet introducing O-glycosylation in human ucOCN also increases its half-life in plasma.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented in Figure 5G-H.

claim: These findings provide an approach to increase recombinant human OCN half-life in vivo, which might be relevant for the future development of OCN-based therapies for human diseases.
source: These findings reveal an important difference between mouse and human OCN biology and also provide an approach to increase recombinant human OCN half-life in vivo, which might be relevant for the future development of OCN-based therapies for human diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.
